Reference: Ahlfeldt et al. (2015)

Model Set-up

The city consists of a set of discrete locations or blocks, which are indexed by i=1,2,...,Si=1,2,...,Si=1,2,...,S. Each block has an effective supply of floor space LiL_iLi​. Floor space can be used commercially or residentially, and we denote the endogenous fractions of floor space allocated to commercial and residential use by θi\theta_iθi​ and 1−θi1-\theta_i1−θi​, respectively.

The city is populated by an endogenous measure of H workers, who are perfectly mobile within the city and the larger economy, which provides a reservation level of utility Uˉ\bar{U}Uˉ. Workers decide whether or not to move to the city before observing idiosyncratic shock for each work-residence pair. If she decides to move into the city, she observes these realizations of the idiosyncratic utility shock.

Workers

First, suppose the utility function for worker ooo residing in block iii and working in block jjj takes the Cobb-Douglas form:

Cijo=Bizijodij(cijoβ)β(lijo1−β)1−β,0<β<1(6.1.6.1)C_{ijo}=\frac{B_iz_{ijo}}{d_{ij}}(\frac{c_{ijo}}{\beta})^{\beta}(\frac{l_{ijo}}{1-\beta})^{1-\beta},\quad 0<\beta<1 \tag{6.1.6.1}Cijo​=dij​Bi​zijo​​(βcijo​​)β(1−βlijo​​)1−β,0<β<1(6.1.6.1)

where cijoc_{ijo}cijo​ is the utility, cijoc_{ijo}cijo​ is the consumption on the final good, and lijol_{ijo}lijo​ is the consumption on the residential floor space. Residential amenities BiB_iBi​ capture common characteristics that make a block a more or less attractive place to live. dijd_{ij}dij​ is the disutility from commuting between iii and jjj. zijoz_{ijo}zijo​ is an idiosyncratic shock that is specific to individual workers and varies with the worker’s blocks of employment and residence. Here the iceberg commuting cost dij=eκτij∈[1,∞)d_{ij}=e^{\kappa\tau_{ij}}\in [1,\infty)dij​=eκτij​∈[1,∞) increases with the travel time τij\tau_{ij}τij​ between blocks iii and jjj. The parameter κ\kappaκ controls the size of commuting costs.

For each worker ooo living in block iii and commuting to block jjj, the idiosyncratic component of utility (zijo)(z_{ijo})(zijo​) is drawn from an independent Fréchet distribution:

F(zijo)=e−TiEjzijo−ε,Ti,Ej>0,  ε>1(6.1.6.2)F(z_{ijo})=e^{-T_iE_jz_{ijo}^{-\varepsilon}},\quad T_i, E_j>0,\;\varepsilon>1 \tag{6.1.6.2}F(zijo​)=e−Ti​Ej​zijo−ε​,Ti​,Ej​>0,ε>1(6.1.6.2)

where the scale parameter Ti>0T_i>0Ti​>0 determines the average utility derived from living in block iii; the scale parameter EjE_jEj​ determines the average utility derived from working in block jjj; and the shape parameter ε>1\varepsilon>1ε>1 controls the dispersion of idiosyncratic utility.

Land Market Clearing

Suppose that ξi≥1\xi_i\geq 1ξi​≥1 captures one plus the tax equivalent of land use regulations that restrict commercial land use relative to residential land use. Land market equilibrium requires no-arbitrage between the commercial and residential use of floor space after the tax equivalent of land use regulations. The share of floor space used commercially (θi\theta_iθi​) is:

Now, we have got εκ\varepsilon\kappaεκ! So cool!

Another 3 parameters cannot be recovered from the data in the study, so we need to use the parameters from previous studies. Consistent with previous literature, the study sets the parameters as:

(1) (1−β)=0.25(1-\beta)=0.25(1−β)=0.25: the share of consumer expenditure on residential floor space (Davis and Weinstein 2002).

(2) (1−α)=0.2(1-\alpha)=0.2(1−α)=0.2: the share of firm expenditure on commercial floor space (Valentinyi and Herrendorf 2008).

(3) (1−μ)=0.25(1-\mu)=0.25(1−μ)=0.25: the share of land in construction costs (Epple, Gordon and Sieg 2010; Combes, Duranton and Gobillon 2012).

Now, we have β\betaβ, α\alphaα, and μ\muμ! So cool!
